terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run your file here to work out tonight's batteries and walk.

tasks.title: Count the batteries
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 1` in `batteries.py`, make a variable called `batteries_needed`: how many batteries fill every head torch, when there are `head_torches` torches and each takes `batteries_per_torch` batteries. Print it to see it.

Check runs your file with other kit in place of the numbers at the top, so build on the names, not on the numbers.
nextSteps: Read tonight's kit near the top of the file.
On the right of `=`, combine the two names with the right operator.
hints: Fourteen torches that each take three batteries need three batteries, fourteen times over.
Python writes "times" as `*`. Both values you need already have names at the top of the file.
The line has the shape `batteries_needed = ... * ...`, with the two names from the kit in place of the dots.

tasks.title: Count the full packs
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 2`, make a variable called `full_packs`: how many whole packs `batteries_needed` fills, when one pack holds `batteries_per_pack` batteries. A pack that is only partly full does not count. Print it to see it.

Check starts Task 2 from `batteries_needed` as Task 1 should make it, and tries numbers that fill the packs exactly, numbers with some left over, too few for one pack, and other pack sizes. `full_packs` must be a whole number.
nextSteps: Divide the batteries by the pack size and look at the result.
Ask what happens to the part after the decimal point.
Pick the division that keeps only the whole packs.
Print it and try 24 and 25 batteries in your head.
hints: Seventeen batteries in packs of eight make two full packs and one battery over. Two is the answer, not 2.125.
Python has two ways to divide. One gives a decimal number, the other gives only the whole times one number fits into the other.
The line has the shape `full_packs = batteries_needed // ...`, with the pack size's name where the dots are.

videos.title: Whole numbers and decimal numbers in Python

tasks.title: Count the loose batteries
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 3`, make a variable called `loose_batteries`: how many batteries are left over once the full packs are filled. Print it to see it.

Check starts Task 3 from `batteries_needed` and `full_packs` as Tasks 1 and 2 should make them, and tries numbers with some left over, none left over, and too few for a whole pack.
nextSteps: Think of 19 batteries in packs of 8: how many are not in a full pack?
Read the part of the lesson on what is left after dividing.
Make `loose_batteries` from the names you already have.
Print it and check it by hand once.
hints: Nineteen in packs of eight leave three over. Twenty-four leave none. Three leave all three.
Python has an operator that gives what is left over after dividing one whole number by another.
The line has the shape `loose_batteries = batteries_needed % ...`, with the pack size's name where the dots are.

tasks.title: Time the walk in
tasks.description:
Under `# Task 4`, make a variable called `walk_in_hours`: how many hours it takes to walk `walk_in_km` kilometres at `walking_speed_kmh` kilometres an hour, rounded to one decimal place. Print it to see it.

Check tries walks that need rounding, walks that come out even and walks of whole hours. `walk_in_hours` must be a decimal number, so a walk of three hours is `3.0`.
nextSteps: Hours are the distance divided by the speed.
Pick the division that keeps the part after the decimal point.
Round the result to one decimal place.
Print it and run the file.
hints: Ten kilometres at three an hour takes a little over three hours. Walking time is not a whole number.
`/` keeps the decimal part. `round` takes a second number in its brackets: how many decimal places to keep.
The line has the shape `walk_in_hours = round(walk_in_km / ..., 1)`, with the speed's name where the dots are.
